subject: tech
title: If This, Then That
about: If this, then that: if it is raining, then take an umbrella; if the light is red, then stop. A plan says what should happen and what comes next, with a goal at the end (K2-AP-05). If-then rules are a bridge topic, since conditionals are taught from Grade 3 on, but a six-year-old already uses them all day, so read it together and let him make up his own rules.
tip: Play if-then at the door: 'If it is raining, then...' and let him finish the rule before you both check the window.

cards.q: If it is raining, then take an umbrella. It is raining. What do you do?
cards.note: A rule has two parts: if this happens, then do that. Rain is the if, umbrella is the then.

cards.q: If it is sunny, then wear a hat. If it is raining, then take an umbrella. It is sunny. What do you do?
cards.note: Two rules. Only the one whose if part is true gets to happen.

cards.q: If the light is red, then stop. The light is red. What do you do?
cards.note: Red is the if. Stop is the then. Cars follow this rule all day.

cards.q: If the light is green, then go. The light turns green. What happens?
cards.note: When the if part comes true, the then part happens.

cards.q: In a game: if you tap the star, then it sparkles. You tap the star. What happens?
cards.note: Games are full of if-then rules. Your tap is the if, the sparkle is the then.

cards.q: In a game: if you tap the star, then it sparkles. You tap the moon. What does the star do?
cards.note: You did not tap the star, so the if part did not happen. No sparkle.

cards.q: If the battery is low, then charge it. The tablet says the battery is low. What do you do?
cards.a: ask a grown-up to charge it
cards.note: The tablet checks its own battery with an if-then rule. Ask a grown-up to plug the charger in.

cards.q: A robot bumps into a wall. Its rule: if you bump, then turn around. What does it do?
cards.note: Robots use if-then rules to decide what to do next.

cards.q: Rule: if it is dark, then turn on the light. It is dark. What happens?
cards.note: Is it dark? is a yes-or-no question. A computer can check it and then act.

cards.q: A computer can check a yes-or-no question. Which one is a yes-or-no question?
cards.note: Yes-or-no questions are easy for computers to check. Then they follow the rule.

cards.q: Before you build, you say what you want to make and what should happen. What is that called?
cards.note: A plan says the goal and what should happen. Programmers plan before they code.

cards.q: Your plan says: the robot should reach the door. What is that part of the plan?
cards.note: The goal is what you want to happen at the end.

cards.q: Rule: if the bell rings, then line up. The bell rings. What comes next?
cards.note: The ring is the if. Lining up is the then. School has lots of if-then rules.

cards.q: Rule: if it is cold, then wear a coat. It is a hot day. What do you wear?
cards.note: The if part did not happen, so the then part does not happen either.

cards.q: You want the light to come on when you clap. Which rule do you write?
cards.note: Put what you check after if, and what should happen after then.

cards.q: If it is a school day, then pack your bag. If it is Saturday, then play. It is Saturday. What do you do?
cards.note: Check each rule. Saturday is not a school day, so only the play rule happens.

cards.q: Rule: if the dog's bowl is empty, then fill it. The bowl is empty. What happens now?
cards.note: Empty bowl is the if, fill it is the then. You just ran an if-then rule!
